hits.draft_en:
A new paper out of China is titled "The End of Harness Engineering", and every agent framework should pay attention.

Core claim: hand-coding the program that wraps a model is no longer a skill worth having.

Why: a human-written harness is a single guess for a single task, made in one afternoon, then left running for months with nobody reading or scoring it.

The alternative is a loop. A small 4B model looks at the failures, suggests 8 edits, and only the one that wins on held-out questions is kept. The large model never changes - the file around it gets rewritten every round.

What's left for people is the scoring set: the questions it gets graded against. Frameworks become throwaway, and writing the exam becomes the work.

Short version: exam first, code second. Guide to the starting harness below ↓

Opus 5.5 cut a studio’s archviz bill from $9,400 a month to $61 in tokens, and the rendering never changed.

The invoice was never the renders. It was the twelve people-hours a week spent turning client notes into scene edits.

> NOTE - a client comment parsed into the objects it affects
> EDIT - materials, placement and lighting changed in the file itself
> DIFF - a before and after render returned with the change listed

Vague feedback is the hard part of that job. Deciding whether a complaint means lighting temperature, material choice or time of day takes judgement, not labour.

That is where the model earns its price. It holds lighting theory, material physics, composition and bpy scripting at once, and a studio normally hires three different people for that spread.

At $4 per million input tokens and $20 out, a full revision round lands under two dollars. The previous round cost a day of someone’s calendar.

Revision cycles were priced on human attention. Nothing about the geometry or the renderer became cheaper.

That is the part studios keep missing when they compare tools. You are not buying faster rendering, you are buying the end of the queue in front of it.

The prompt that runs all of it is in the video.

THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 at once, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

4. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: delegate every repo search and test run to the Haiku 5.5 subagents to keep the main context small.

outsiders.text:
THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 at once, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

4. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: delegate every repo search and test run to the Haiku 5.5 subagents to keep the main context small.
5. Route fast deterministic forks (tool choice, path selection, retries) through JEV.
